doc.title: Josiah Gluck interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 13, 2022

title: What makes a good mix, broadcast limits and surround sound
summary: A good mix lets him hear vocal, bass and ride cymbal; he discusses loudness standards and why SNL changed its surround approach.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Do you have — of course you have the house band and then you have the live music guest. Do you have something in your head, in your hearing that matches them in the sense that overall volume, bass volume, all that kind of thing?

Well you know I’ve always liked to say that on the spectrum of mixes like you can say well this is wrong and this is right, and everything else on either side of it is personal taste. But you want to hear the vocal. You want to hear the bass. To me a mix works when I’m hearing the bass and I can see and hear the drummer on the ride cymbal. I hear that whole spectrum. I see and hear the whole spectrum. So that to me is very important. As far as overall level, we’re locked into certain broadcast standards of how loud you can be and then you’re playing games with compression and apparent loudness and then there’s also the questions of mixing in surround sound and do you do it in surround. We have modified our approach to surround sound over the past few seasons primarily

because of where the vocal sits in the guest band mixes, how things fold down to stereo on YouTube or someone who’s not watching on YouTube or that person who’s standing next to me on the subway on Monday morning watching the show that way. So I also feel, I mean I love mixing in surround but I also feel that it affords the home user, sometimes 5.1, opportunities to completely wreck my mix. So you can only protect how well it sounds leaving you, leaving the studio.
